theme: The LORD reigns; let the peoples tremble
readingInstruction: Read Psalm 99. You will read it again later in the plan. Read it now as a hymn of the holy God who answers prayer. Notice the refrain “Holy is he.”
settingTheScene: Psalm 99 is the last of the “LORD reigns” psalms. It has a threefold refrain: “Holy is he” (vv. 3, 5) and “Holy is the LORD our God” (v. 9). It recalls Moses, Aaron, and Samuel as those who called on God and were answered. Coming right before the prophet Haggai, who will call the people to build the temple, it is a good reminder of the holiness of the place where God meets his people.
observation: “The LORD reigns; let the peoples tremble! He sits enthroned upon the cherubim; let the earth quake!” (v. 1).
“The LORD is great in Zion; he is exalted over all the peoples” (v. 2).
“Let them praise your great and awesome name! Holy is he!” (v. 3).
“The King in his might loves justice. You have established equity; you have executed justice and righteousness in Jacob” (v. 4).
“Exalt the LORD our God; worship at his footstool! Holy is he!” (v. 5).
“Moses and Aaron were among his priests, Samuel also was among those who called upon his name. They called to the LORD, and he answered them” (v. 6).
“You were a forgiving God to them, but an avenger of their wrongdoings” (v. 8).
“Exalt the LORD our God, and worship at his holy mountain; for the LORD our God is holy!” (v. 9).
interpretation:
The psalm begins with God’s majesty. He sits enthroned on the cherubim, which refers to the ark’s mercy seat. He is great in Zion and exalted over all peoples. The proper response is trembling. Holiness is not just moral purity but God’s otherness, his set-apartness, the fact that he is not like us.

The first refrain, “Holy is he,” appears after the call to praise his name. The second appears after the call to worship at his footstool, the temple or ark. The third appears at the end. These three refrains remind us of Isaiah’s vision of the seraphim, who cried “Holy, holy, holy.” This psalm gives the three-fold chant in a different form.

In the center, the psalm says that the strong King loves justice. His holiness is not cold but moral. He establishes equity. A holy God is a just God.

Then comes a surprise. This awesome, holy God answers prayer. “Moses and Aaron… Samuel… called to the LORD, and he answered them.” He spoke to them in the pillar of cloud and gave them his testimonies. The God who sits on the cherubim is the God who speaks to his servants. Holiness and nearness are not opposed.

And then the key line: “You were a forgiving God to them, but an avenger of their wrongdoings.” Moses interceded and was heard, yet there were consequences. God’s forgiveness does not erase reality. This is the pattern of the exile: he forgave, yet the people bore the discipline.

For the returned community, the temple was a holy place to be approached with reverence. The message of Haggai is coming: build the house, because the holy God will dwell there. And for us, the holiness is met by the cross.
connection: Isaiah 6:3: “Holy, holy, holy is the LORD of hosts.” Revelation 4:8 repeats the threefold holy around the throne. 1 Peter 1:15-16: “You shall be holy, for I am holy.” Hebrews 4:14-16: we have a great high priest who sympathizes with our weaknesses. Hebrews 12:28-29: let us offer acceptable worship with reverence and awe. James 5:16-18: the prayer of a righteous person has great power.
application:
Pause before prayer and remember who you are addressing: the holy God who sits enthroned.

Remember that you can approach him in Christ, and call on him as Moses, Aaron, and Samuel did.

Ask where you have treated God casually, and recover reverence.
prayerPrompts: Tremble before the God who reigns.
Thank him that he answered those who called on him.
